reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing, highly vascular paraganglioma arising from paraganglionic tissue around the jugular bulb at the skull base
Pulsatile tinnitus and conductive hearing loss are common early symptoms, often with a red-blue retrotympanic mass behind the eardrum
Growth into the jugular foramen produces lower cranial nerve palsies (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory and hypoglossal), the jugular foramen syndrome
A minority are functionally active and secrete catecholamines, so a secretory phenotype should be screened for before intervention
Multiple or familial paragangliomas occur, particularly with succinate dehydrogenase gene mutations, warranting genetic evaluation
MRI classically shows a 'salt-and-pepper' appearance from flow voids, while CT demonstrates the irregular, moth-eaten erosion of the jugular foramen
Because of intense vascularity, biopsy is generally avoided and preoperative angiography with embolisation is often used before surgery
Management is individualised between microsurgical resection, stereotactic radiosurgery or radiotherapy, and observation, balancing tumour control against cranial nerve morbidity
reference.pathophysiology: Glomus jugulare tumours are paragangliomas derived from neural-crest paraganglion cells associated with the autonomic nervous system near the jugular bulb and adjacent Jacobson and Arnold nerves. They are typically benign but locally invasive, spreading along paths of least resistance through the temporal bone, jugular foramen and middle ear, and eroding bone as they enlarge. Their rich vascularity accounts for the pulsatile tinnitus and the risk of haemorrhage with biopsy. A subset secrete catecholamines, and germline mutations, especially in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes, predispose to multifocal and familial disease.
additionalDifferentials: Glomus tympanicum tumour confined to the middle ear
Aberrant internal carotid artery or high jugular bulb
Meningioma or schwannoma of the jugular foramen
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the skull base showing characteristic flow voids
High-resolution temporal bone CT to assess bony erosion of the jugular foramen
Catecholamine and metanephrine screening to detect a secretory tumour
Angiography with consideration of preoperative embolisation
Genetic testing for succinate dehydrogenase and related mutations, with screening for multifocal disease
redFlags: Progressive lower cranial nerve palsies causing hoarseness, dysphagia or aspiration
Symptoms or biochemical evidence of catecholamine secretion
Intracranial extension with brainstem or cerebellar compression
Rapid growth or features suggesting rare malignant paraganglioma
reference.prognosis: As a predominantly benign but locally aggressive tumour, prognosis for survival is generally good, and slow growth may allow observation in selected older patients. Treatment aims for durable control while preserving cranial nerve function; surgery and radiotherapy each achieve high control rates, though cranial nerve deficits can be permanent and recurrence or new tumours may occur, especially in hereditary disease.
pitfalls: Performing biopsy of a vascular retrotympanic mass and precipitating significant bleeding
Failing to screen for catecholamine secretion before surgery or embolisation
Overlooking a hereditary syndrome and coexisting paragangliomas or phaeochromocytoma
Underestimating the cranial nerve morbidity of aggressive resection in slow-growing tumours
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Microsurgical resection for definitive control, or stereotactic radiosurgery and radiotherapy to achieve tumour control while preserving cranial nerve function
Observation with serial imaging is reasonable for small, slow-growing tumours in older or comorbid patients
Preoperative angiography with embolisation to reduce the vascularity and bleeding risk of resection
Screen for catecholamine secretion and, if a secretory tumour is confirmed, establish alpha-adrenergic blockade before any intervention
Cranial nerve rehabilitation with swallowing and voice therapy for the lower cranial nerve deficits of jugular foramen syndrome
Offer genetic testing for succinate dehydrogenase mutations with screening for multifocal or familial paraganglioma
Manage through a skull base multidisciplinary team with long-term surveillance imaging
